title.zh: 气血不足的科学调理：中医补气养血全攻略
title.en: Scientific Qi-Blood Tonification: Complete TCM Guide

description.zh: 深入解析气血不足的中医机理、临床表现、形成原因及系统调理方案，结合经典方剂与现代研究，提供科学有效的养生指导
description.en: Comprehensive analysis of Qi-Blood deficiency with TCM mechanisms, clinical manifestations, causes, and systematic conditioning plans

zh.text: 气血是维持人体生命活动的两大基本物质，二者一阴一阳、一主动一主濡，共同维系着人体的正常生理功能。《灵枢·营卫生会》有云："人受气于谷，谷入于胃，以传与肺，五脏六腑皆以受气。"气具备推动、温煦、防御、固摄、气化等多重功能，犹如人体的"发动机"；血则承载营养精微物质，濡养全身脏腑组织，如同"灌溉系统"。气为血之帅——气能生血、行血、摄血；血为气之母——血能载气、养气。二者相互依存、相互转化，共同构成了人体生命活动的物质基础。气血失调是中医临床最常见的病理状态，可以说"气血不和，百病乃变化而生"（《素问·调经论》）。本文将从理论基础到临床实践，系统介绍气血不足的全面调理方案。
一、气血不足的中医理论基础
气的概念与功能

气是构成人体和维持生命活动的精微物质，具有极其丰富的内涵。《素问·六节藏象论》曰："气者，人之根本也。"气在人体内有不同的分布和功能表现。元气源于先天之精，是生命的本源动力，藏于肾中，推动着人体的生长发育和各脏腑的功能活动。宗气积聚于胸中，由肺吸入的清气和脾胃运化而来的水谷精气合化而成，贯注心肺以推动呼吸和血液运行。营气行于脉中，具有营养全身的作用，是血液的重要组成部分。卫气行于脉外，功能如"卫戍"一般，护卫肌表、抵御外邪、调节体温。这四种气既有区别又相互联系，共同维持着人体的生命活动。临床上常说的"气虚"，往往涉及的是整体气机功能的减退，以元气和宗气不足最为常见。
血的概念与功能

血是循行于脉中的红色液态物质，由脾胃运化的水谷精微化生而来。《素问·调经论》精辟地概括了血的生成与运行："血者，水谷之精也，生于脾，藏于肝，输于心，布于肺，统于脾。"血的生理功能主要体现在三个方面。首先是营养作用——血循脉行于全身，为五脏六腑、经络骨骼、四肢百骸提供必需的营养物质。其次是滋润作用——血能濡养皮肤、毛发、黏膜和肌肉，使其保持润泽和弹性，这也是"血虚生风、血燥生痒"在皮肤疾病中的病理基础。其三是精神活动的物质基础——心血充足则神志清晰、精神充沛，正如《灵枢·平人绝谷》所言"血脉和利，精神乃居"；反之，血虚则神疲健忘、失眠多梦。
气血关系

气和血的关系可以用"气为血之帅，血为气之母"十个字来概括。气能生血——水谷精微在气的运化作用下转化为血，临床上补血时常配补气之品，正是取"气能生血"之意，如当归补血汤中黄芪五倍于当归。气能行血——血液的运行依赖气的推动，气虚或气滞均可导致血行不畅，称为"气虚血瘀"或"气滞血瘀"。气能摄血——气对血液有统摄作用，使其循行脉中而不溢出脉外，气虚固摄无权则会导致各种出血。另一方面，血能载气——气必须依附于血液才能运行全身，这就是为什么大失血时会出现"气随血脱"的危重证候。血能养气——气在体内不断消耗，需要依靠血液中的营养物质来补充。二者如影随形、不可分割，临床调理气血时必须兼顾而不能偏废。
二、气血不足的临床表现
气虚的典型症状

气虚的本质是全身或某个脏腑功能活动的减退。《医宗金鉴》指出："气虚者，补之以甘温。"气虚的临床表现可以从四个方面把握。全身症状方面，患者常感神疲乏力、少气懒言、头晕目眩，稍微活动就觉得累，正所谓"劳则气耗"。体表症状方面，面色苍白或萎黄，动则自汗，且因为卫气不固而容易感冒。消化系统方面，食欲不振、腹胀便溏，这是因为脾主运化，脾气虚则运化无力。舌脉方面，舌淡胖大、边有齿痕，脉象虚弱无力。我在临床上接诊的气虚患者中，最多的主诉就是"总是觉得很累，睡醒也解不了乏"，这正是气虚最典型的感觉。
血虚的典型症状

血虚的本质是血液不足，脏腑组织失于濡养。《景岳全书》云："血不足以濡脏腑，则面色萎黄，肌肉消瘦。"血虚的表现同样涵盖多个方面。全身症状以头晕眼花、心悸失眠、健忘多梦为主，这是因为心血不足则神无所依、肝血不足则魂不守舍。体表症状非常直观——面色萎黄或苍白、唇甲色淡无华、毛发干枯易断，一眼望去便给人以"血色不足"之感。女性患者最突出的表现是月经量少、色淡、周期延长甚至闭经。舌质淡白、脉象细弱是血虚的典型舌脉特征。需要特别指出的是，血虚的诊断不能仅凭一两个症状，要综合全身表现进行判断，临床上很多被误认为"贫血"的患者其实并不符合血虚的诊断标准。
气血两虚的综合表现

在临床实践中，气虚和血虚往往不是孤立存在的，而是相互影响、相互加重，最终形成气血两虚的复杂证候。这类患者既有气虚的神疲乏力、少气懒言、自汗怕风，又有血虚的头晕眼花、心悸失眠、面色萎黄。两者交织在一起，呈现出比单纯气虚或血虚更为复杂的临床表现。我在临床上有一个深刻的体会：很多年轻女性患者因为节食减肥导致的气血两虚，面色又黄又白、说话有气无力、月经稀发或闭经，这种状态靠单一的补气或补血都是不够的，必须气血双补，同时纠正不当的饮食习惯，才能从根本上恢复。
三、气血不足的形成原因

气血不足的形成原因多种多样，可以归纳为先天和后天两大类。先天禀赋不足是指父母体质虚弱，遗传基因中决定了气血偏弱的基础。后天因素则更为复杂：饮食失宜——不规律进食、节食减肥、脾胃功能虚弱，导致气血生化无源；过度劳累——长期超负荷工作、熬夜、思虑过度，耗伤气血；情志失调——长期焦虑、抑郁、情绪波动大，肝气郁结则暗耗气血；久病耗损——慢性疾病如结核、肿瘤、自身免疫病等，长期消耗人体的精微物质；失血过多——外伤大出血、月经过多、产后失血等直接导致血液亏耗。在接诊时我通常会仔细询问患者的生活方式，因为在现代社会中，绝大多数气血不足的根源都在于"后天失养"——不是吃得太差，而是吃得不规律、睡得太晚、想得太多。改善了这些因素，调理气血才能事半功倍。
四、经典补气养血方剂
中医在两千年的临床实践中积累了丰富的补气养血方剂，这些方剂经历了无数医家的反复验证，是调理气血的可靠武器。需要强调的是，方剂的使用必须在中医辨证指导下进行，不可自行对号入座。
补气方剂

四君子汤出自《太平惠民和剂局方》，由人参、白术、茯苓、甘草四味组成，是益气健脾的祖方，几乎所有补气方剂都是在它的基础上加减化裁而来。方中人参大补元气为君，白术健脾燥湿为臣，茯苓健脾渗湿为佐，甘草调和诸药为使，四药合用，补而不滞、温而不燥。补中益气汤出自金元四大家李东垣的《脾胃论》，在四君子基础上加入黄芪、升麻、柴胡等，长于补中益气、升阳举陷，适用于中气下陷所致的胃下垂、脱肛、子宫脱垂等。玉屏风散由黄芪、白术、防风三味组成，虽然只有三味药，但配伍精妙——黄芪益气固表、白术健脾助卫、防风走表祛风，共同起到益气固表止汗的作用，特别适合容易感冒、自汗的气虚体质者日常调理。
补血方剂

四物汤出自《太平惠民和剂局方》，由当归、熟地、白芍、川芎四味组成，是补血活血的基础方，被誉为"妇科第一方"。值得注意的是，四物汤并非单纯的补血方剂——其中当归补血活血、熟地滋阴补血、白芍养血柔肝、川芎活血行气，四药配伍实现了"补而不滞、活而不散"的精妙平衡。当归补血汤虽只有当归和黄芪两味药，但配伍比例独具匠心——黄芪用量五倍于当归，取"有形之血不能速生，无形之气所当急固"之义，通过大补元气来促进血液生成。归脾汤出自《济生方》，方中白术、茯神、黄芪、龙眼肉、酸枣仁、人参等配伍，既能益气健脾以生血，又能养心安神以定志，适用于心脾两虚所致的气血不足、失眠健忘。
气血双补方剂

当气虚和血虚同时存在时，就需要气血双补的方剂。八珍汤是四君子汤和四物汤的合方，兼具益气健脾和补血活血的双重功效，是气血双补最经典的方剂，适用于面色萎黄、头晕目眩、四肢倦怠、气短懒言等气血两虚证。十全大补汤在八珍汤基础上加了黄芪和肉桂两味，黄芪增强补气之力，肉桂温阳以助气血生化，温补之力更强，适合偏阳虚体质的气血不足患者。人参养荣汤则在补气养血的基础上更侧重于养心安神，适合气血两虚伴有明显失眠健忘、心神不安者。这些方剂各有侧重，临证选择时需仔细辨析。
五、常用补气养血食材
药食同源是中医养生的一大特色。日常饮食中合理搭配补气养血的食材，既能满足口腹之欲，又能达到养生保健的目的。
补气食材

黄芪被《本草纲目》列为补气第一要药，性味甘温，能补气升阳、固表止汗、利水消肿。日常可用黄芪片泡水或煲汤，每次10至15克即可，但因药性偏温，阴虚火旺者不宜。党参是参类中最平和的补气药，补中益气、健脾益肺，价格适中，适合日常食疗。山药既是食物又是药物，《神农本草经》将其列为上品，"补中益气力，长肌肉，久服耳目聪明"，脾胃虚弱者可长期食用。红枣补中益气、养血安神，民间有"日食三枣，青春不老"之说，每日食用3至5颗即可。桂圆补益心脾、养血安神，是气血两虚伴失眠者的食疗佳品。鸡肉温中益气，适合产后、术后、久病体虚者调补。
补血食材

当归是补血第一要药，《本草纲目》称其"治头痛、心腹诸痛，润肠胃筋骨皮肤"，其独特的补血兼活血之性使其在补血食材中独树一帜。我常建议血虚患者每周用当归15克与鸡肉或排骨炖汤食用。阿胶由驴皮熬制而成，补血滋阴、润燥止血的功效极为突出，是治疗血虚证的"王牌"药材。但需注意，阿胶滋腻碍胃，脾胃虚弱、消化不良者不宜单独大量服用，可配合理气健脾的药物同用。枸杞滋补肝肾、益精明目，嚼服或泡水均有补血养肝之功，每日15至20克为佳。黑芝麻补肝肾、益精血，《本草备要》称其"补肝肾，润五脏，填精髓"，适合长期食用。猪肝补肝明目、养血，菠菜养血止血，二者同煮汤食用，对缺铁性贫血有较好的食疗效果。
六、补气养血药膳方
药膳是中医药文化中"寓医于食"的集中体现，将药物治疗和日常饮食巧妙结合。以下三个药膳方是我在临床中经常推荐给患者的，适合家庭制作，安全有效。

zh.title: 当归黄芪炖鸡汤
zh.instructions:
1. 老母鸡切块，焯水去血沫
2. 当归、黄芪用清水冲洗干净
3. 所有材料放入砂锅，加入足量清水
4. 大火烧开后转小火慢炖2小时
5. 加盐调味即可
6. 功效：补气养血，适合气血两虚者

zh.text: 此方是气血双补的代表性药膳，黄芪补气、当归补血、红枣和桂圆养血安神，老母鸡温中益气。我在临床中观察到，气血不足的患者每周食用此汤1至2次，坚持一个月后，面色红润程度、精力和体力都有明显改善。

zh.title: 桂圆红枣粥
zh.instructions:
1. 大米淘洗干净，提前浸泡30分钟
2. 桂圆肉、红枣洗净
3. 所有材料放入锅中，加水煮粥
4. 大火烧开后转小火煮20分钟
5. 加入红糖调味即可
6. 功效：补益心脾，养血安神

zh.title: 山药枸杞排骨汤
zh.instructions:
1. 排骨切块焯水
2. 山药去皮切块
3. 排骨、生姜、葱段放入砂锅，加水烧开
4. 转小火炖1小时，加入山药、枸杞
5. 再炖20分钟，加盐调味
6. 功效：益气养阴，健脾补肾

zh.text: 七、补气养血穴位按摩

穴位按摩是补气养血不可或缺的辅助手段。足三里（ST36）位于小腿外侧、犊鼻下3寸，是足阳明胃经的合穴，也是全身最重要的强壮穴之一，有"常按足三里，胜吃老母鸡"之说，按揉此穴可补中益气、健脾和胃。气海穴（CV6）位于腹部正中线脐下1.5寸，是元气汇聚之处，手掌按揉顺时针方向36圈有补气固本之功。血海穴（SP10）位于大腿内侧、髌底内侧端上2寸，是调血的要穴，按揉可补血养血、活血化瘀，尤其适合女性气血不足、月经不调者。三阴交（SP6）位于小腿内侧内踝尖上3寸，是肝脾肾三经的交会穴，调补气血、调理肝肾的效果非常显著。膈俞穴（BL17）位于背部第七胸椎棘突下旁开1.5寸，是八会穴中的"血会"，专治与血相关的各种问题。这些穴位每日各按揉1至2分钟，坚持一段时间后可显著改善气血运行。
八、生活调理建议

调理气血，生活方式的重要性不亚于方药。《素问·上古天真论》提出了"食饮有节，起居有常，不妄作劳"的养生总原则，至今仍是气血调理的基石。规律作息是第一要务——晚上11点前入睡，保证7至8小时的高质量睡眠，因为夜间是人体气血修复和再生的黄金时间。适度运动可以帮助气血运行，但气血不足者不宜剧烈运动，散步、慢跑、太极、八段锦等温和运动最为适宜。情绪调节不容忽视——肝气郁结是气血失调的重要诱因，保持心情舒畅、避免过度思虑是"不花钱的良药"。饮食上三餐规律、营养均衡，多吃补气养血的食物。注意劳逸结合，不过度透支身体。适当晒太阳有助于维生素D的合成，对钙吸收和整体健康也有帮助。
九、现代研究支持

中医补气养血的科学内涵正在被现代研究所揭示。黄芪多糖是黄芪的核心活性成分，研究表明其能增强机体的免疫功能、促进造血干细胞的增殖和分化，从而改善贫血状态。当归中的阿魏酸具有明确的抗氧化、抗炎和抗血小板聚集作用，这与中医"当归补血活血"的传统认识高度吻合。阿胶的现代药理研究证实，其能促进红细胞和血红蛋白的生成，提高血清铁含量，对缺铁性贫血和失血性贫血都有明确的改善作用。穴位按摩方面，研究表明刺激足三里等穴位可以调节神经内分泌系统、改善局部和全身的微循环。这些研究成果为中医补气养血理论提供了现代科学证据，也让我们更加确信——中医药是一座值得深入挖掘的宝库。
本文内容仅供科普参考，不能替代专业医疗诊断。气血调理需在中医师辨证指导下进行，特别是严重气血不足者应配合药物治疗，不可仅依赖食疗和自我调理。

en.text: Qi and Blood are the two fundamental substances sustaining human life activities. One represents yang (active, warming), the other yin (nourishing, moistening), and together they maintain normal physiological functions. As stated in the Lingshu: "Humans receive Qi from food. Food enters the stomach, transforms through the lungs, and all five zang and six fu organs receive Qi." Qi possesses multiple functions including propulsion, warming, defense, consolidation, and transformation — it functions like the body's "engine." Blood carries nutritive substances, nourishing all organs and tissues throughout the body — it serves as the "irrigation system." Qi commands Blood — Qi generates, moves, and contains Blood. Blood nourishes Qi — Blood carries and sustains Qi. They depend on each other and transform mutually, forming the material foundation of life activities. Qi-Blood disharmony is the most common pathological condition in TCM clinical practice — as the Su Wen states, "When Qi and Blood are disharmonious, a hundred diseases arise." This article presents a comprehensive approach to Qi-Blood regulation, from theoretical foundations to clinical practice.
1. TCM Theoretical Foundation of Qi-Blood Deficiency
Concept and Functions of Qi

Qi is the fundamental substance that composes the human body and maintains life activities, with exceptionally rich connotations. The Su Wen states: "Qi is the root of the human being." Qi has different distributions and functions within the body. Original Qi (Yuan Qi) derives from congenital essence, stored in the kidney, serving as the fundamental driving force for growth, development, and the functional activities of all organs. Gathering Qi (Zong Qi) accumulates in the chest, formed by the combination of clean air inhaled by the lung and the essence of food transformed by the spleen and stomach — it pours into the heart and lung to propel respiration and blood circulation. Nutritive Qi (Ying Qi) flows within the vessels, nourishing the entire body, and is an important component of blood. Defensive Qi (Wei Qi) flows outside the vessels, acting like a "garrison" that protects the body surface, resists external pathogens, and regulates body temperature. These four types of Qi, distinct yet interconnected, collectively sustain life activities. What is clinically referred to as "Qi deficiency" typically involves the overall decline of Qi function, most commonly manifesting as insufficiency of Original Qi and Gathering Qi.
Concept and Functions of Blood

Blood is a red liquid substance that circulates within the vessels, transformed from the essence of food by the spleen and stomach. The Su Wen brilliantly summarizes the generation and circulation of blood: "Blood is the essence of food and water. It is generated in the spleen, stored in the liver, circulated by the heart, distributed by the lung, and governed by the spleen." The physiological functions of blood manifest in three primary aspects. First, nourishment — blood circulates throughout the body via the vessels, providing essential nutrients to the five zang and six fu organs, meridians, bones, and limbs. Second, moistening — blood nourishes the skin, hair, mucous membranes, and muscles, maintaining their moisture and elasticity. This is also the pathological basis of conditions like "blood deficiency generating wind" and "blood dryness causing itching" in dermatology. Third, the material basis of mental activity — sufficient heart blood ensures clear consciousness and abundant energy, as the Lingshu states, "when blood and vessels are harmonious, the spirit resides." Conversely, blood deficiency leads to fatigue, forgetfulness, insomnia, and excessive dreaming.
Qi-Blood Relationship

The relationship between Qi and Blood can be summarized in the principle: "Qi is the commander of Blood, and Blood is the mother of Qi." Qi generates Blood — the essence of food is transformed into blood through the transformative function of Qi. This is why Qi-tonifying herbs are often added when treating Blood deficiency, exemplified by Dang Gui Bu Xue Tang where Astragalus is used at five times the dose of Angelica. Qi moves Blood — blood circulation depends on the propelling force of Qi; Qi deficiency or Qi stagnation can both cause poor blood flow, termed "Qi deficiency with blood stasis" or "Qi stagnation with blood stasis." Qi contains Blood — Qi has a consolidating function that keeps blood within the vessels; when Qi deficiency impairs this function, various types of bleeding can occur. On the other hand, Blood carries Qi — Qi must be attached to blood to circulate throughout the body, which is why massive blood loss can lead to the critical condition of "Qi escaping with blood." Blood nourishes Qi — Qi is continuously consumed and must be replenished by nutrients carried in the blood. The two are as inseparable as shadow and form; clinical treatment of Qi and Blood must address both simultaneously.
2. Clinical Manifestations of Qi-Blood Deficiency
Typical Qi Deficiency Symptoms

The essence of Qi deficiency is the decline of overall or organ-specific functional activity. The Golden Mirror of Medicine states: "For Qi deficiency, use sweet and warm herbs to tonify." The clinical manifestations can be understood from four dimensions. Systemically, patients commonly experience fatigue, weak voice, shortness of breath, and dizziness — activities quickly exhaust them, confirming the principle that "fatigue consumes Qi." Externally, the complexion appears pale or sallow, with spontaneous sweating upon minimal exertion, and frequent colds due to impaired defensive Qi. Digestively, poor appetite, abdominal distension, and loose stool occur because the spleen governs transportation and the spleen Qi lacks strength. On the tongue and pulse, the tongue is pale and swollen with tooth marks, and the pulse is weak and forceless. In my clinical practice, the most common complaint from Qi-deficient patients is: "I always feel tired, and sleep doesn't restore my energy" — this is the hallmark sensation of Qi deficiency.
Typical Blood Deficiency Symptoms

The essence of Blood deficiency is insufficient blood volume, depriving organs and tissues of nourishment. The Jing Yue Quan Shu states: "When blood is insufficient to moisten the organs, the complexion becomes sallow and muscles wither." The manifestations span multiple areas. Systemic symptoms include dizziness, blurred vision, palpitations, insomnia, and excessive dreaming — heart blood deficiency deprives the spirit of its abode, while liver blood deficiency prevents the ethereal soul from residing. External signs are highly visible — sallow or pale complexion, lusterless lips and nails, dry and brittle hair — one glance conveys a sense of "insufficient blood." The most prominent presentation in female patients is scanty, pale menstruation, delayed cycles, or even amenorrhea. A pale tongue and thin, fine pulse are the characteristic tongue and pulse findings. It deserves special emphasis that the diagnosis of blood deficiency should not be based on one or two symptoms alone but requires comprehensive assessment of systemic manifestations — many patients mistakenly labeled as having "anemia" do not actually meet the diagnostic criteria for blood deficiency.
Combined Qi-Blood Deficiency

In clinical practice, Qi deficiency and Blood deficiency rarely occur in isolation. They interact and mutually exacerbate each other, eventually forming a combined pattern of dual deficiency. These patients present with both the fatigue, weak voice, spontaneous sweating, and wind aversion of Qi deficiency, and the dizziness, palpitations, insomnia, and sallow complexion of Blood deficiency. The symptoms intertwine, producing a more complex clinical picture than either pattern alone. I have a profound clinical observation: many young women who develop combined Qi-Blood deficiency from crash dieting present with a complexion that is both sallow and pale, speak with barely audible voices, and have infrequent menstruation or amenorrhea. This condition cannot be corrected by tonifying Qi or Blood alone — both must be addressed simultaneously, and the underlying disordered eating habits must be corrected for fundamental recovery.
3. Causes of Qi-Blood Deficiency

The causes of Qi-Blood deficiency are diverse and can be categorized into congenital and acquired factors. Congenital deficiency refers to a constitutionally weak foundation inherited from parents with inherently weak Qi and Blood. Acquired factors are more complex: improper diet — irregular eating, crash dieting, or weak spleen-stomach function impairs the generation of Qi and Blood; overexertion — chronic overwork, sleep deprivation, and excessive mental activity consume Qi and Blood; emotional imbalance — chronic anxiety, depression, and significant mood fluctuations deplete Qi and Blood through liver Qi stagnation; chronic illness — diseases such as tuberculosis, cancer, and autoimmune conditions that persistently consume the body's nutritive substances; excessive blood loss — trauma, heavy menstruation, and postpartum hemorrhage directly deplete blood volume. When consulting patients, I always carefully inquire about lifestyle factors because in modern society, the root of most Qi-Blood deficiencies lies in "acquired neglect" — not eating poorly, but eating irregularly; not lacking food, but sleeping too late and thinking too much. When these factors are corrected, Qi-Blood regulation becomes far more effective.
4. Classical Qi-Blood Tonifying Formulas

Over two thousand years of clinical practice, TCM has accumulated a wealth of Qi-Blood tonifying formulas, each tested and validated by generations of physicians. These formulas are proven tools for regulating Qi and Blood. However, it must be emphasized that formula selection requires proper TCM pattern differentiation — self-prescribing without guidance is not advisable.
Qi-Tonifying Formulas

Si Jun Zi Tang (Four Gentlemen Decoction), from the Tai Ping Hui Min He Ji Ju Fang, consists of Ginseng, Atractylodes, Poria, and Licorice. It is the foundational formula for tonifying Qi and strengthening the Spleen, from which nearly all Qi-tonifying formulas are derived through modification. Ginseng greatly tonifies Yuan Qi as the chief ingredient, Atractylodes strengthens the Spleen and dries dampness as the deputy, Poria strengthens the Spleen and drains dampness as the assistant, and Licorice harmonizes the formula as the envoy — the combination is tonifying without causing stagnation, warming without causing dryness. Bu Zhong Yi Qi Tang (Supplement the Middle and Boost Qi Decoction), from Li Dongyuan's Pi Wei Lun, adds Astragalus, Cimicifuga, and Bupleurum to the Four Gentlemen base, excelling at tonifying the middle Qi and raising sunken Yang — it is indicated for gastroparesis, rectal prolapse, and uterine prolapse due to sinking of middle Qi. Yu Ping Feng San (Jade Screen Powder), composed of just Astragalus, Atractylodes, and Saposhnikovia, is a masterfully designed formula — Astragalus tonifies Qi and secures the exterior, Atractylodes strengthens the Spleen and assists defensive Qi, and Saposhnikovia dispels wind from the exterior — together they tonify Qi, secure the exterior, and stop sweating, making it ideal for daily regulation in Qi-deficient individuals prone to colds and spontaneous sweating.
Blood-Tonifying Formulas

Si Wu Tang (Four Substances Decoction), also from the Tai Ping Hui Min He Ji Ju Fang, consists of Angelica, Prepared Rehmannia, White Peony, and Chuanxiong. It is the foundational formula for tonifying and activating Blood and is known as the "first formula for gynecology." It is worth noting that Si Wu Tang is not a purely blood-tonifying formula — Angelica tonifies and activates blood, Prepared Rehmannia nourishes yin and tonifies blood, White Peony nourishes blood and softens the liver, and Chuanxiong activates blood and moves Qi — achieving a delicate balance of "tonifying without stagnation, activating without dissipation." Dang Gui Bu Xue Tang (Angelica Blood-Tonifying Decoction) contains only Angelica and Astragalus, but the ratio is ingeniously designed — Astragalus at five times the dose of Angelica, following the principle that "physical blood cannot be rapidly generated, while insubstantial Qi must be urgently secured," promoting blood production through greatly tonifying Yuan Qi. Gui Pi Tang (Restore the Spleen Decoction), from the Ji Sheng Fang, combines Atractylodes, Poria, Astragalus, Longan, Sour Jujube Seed, and Ginseng to tonify Qi and strengthen the Spleen for blood generation while nourishing the heart and calming the spirit — it is indicated for Qi-Blood deficiency with insomnia and forgetfulness due to dual deficiency of heart and spleen.
Dual Qi-Blood Tonifying Formulas

When Qi deficiency and Blood deficiency coexist, formulas that tonify both simultaneously are needed. Ba Zhen Tang (Eight Precious Decoction) is the combination of Si Jun Zi Tang and Si Wu Tang, possessing both the functions of tonifying Qi and strengthening the Spleen and of tonifying and activating Blood. It is the most classic formula for dual Qi-Blood tonification, indicated for sallow complexion, dizziness, fatigue, shortness of breath, and weak voice. Shi Quan Da Bu Tang (Ten Complete Great Tonification Decoction) adds Astragalus and Cinnamon to Ba Zhen Tang — Astragalus enhances Qi-tonifying power, and Cinnamon warms Yang to assist Qi-Blood generation, making it suitable for Qi-Blood deficiency patients with a tendency toward Yang deficiency. Ren Shen Yang Rong Tang (Ginseng Nutritive Decoction), while tonifying Qi and Blood, places greater emphasis on nourishing the heart and calming the spirit, making it suitable for Qi-Blood deficiency with prominent insomnia, forgetfulness, and mental restlessness. Each of these formulas has its specific emphasis, and careful differentiation is required for proper clinical selection.
5. Common Qi-Blood Tonifying Foods

The principle of "medicine and food sharing the same origin" is a distinctive feature of TCM health preservation. Incorporating Qi-Blood tonifying foods into the daily diet allows one to enjoy meals while achieving health maintenance purposes.
Qi-Tonifying Foods

Astragalus is ranked as the foremost Qi-tonifying herb in the Ben Cao Gang Mu. Sweet and warm in nature, it tonifies Qi and raises Yang, secures the exterior and stops sweating, and promotes urination to reduce edema. For daily use, steep 10 to 15 grams of Astragalus slices in water or add to soups. However, due to its warm nature, it is not suitable for those with Yin deficiency and internal heat. Codonopsis is the gentlest of the ginseng family for Qi tonification, tonifying the middle Qi and strengthening the Spleen and Lung. It is moderately priced and suitable for daily dietary therapy. Yam is both food and medicine, classified as a top-grade herb in the Shen Nong Ben Cao Jing — "tonifying the middle, increasing strength, and with prolonged use, sharpening hearing and eyesight." Those with weak Spleen and Stomach can consume it long-term. Red dates tonify the middle Qi and nourish the Blood, inspiring the folk saying "three dates a day keep aging away" — 3 to 5 daily are sufficient. Longan benefits the Heart and Spleen, nourishes Blood and calms the spirit, making it an excellent dietary remedy for Qi-Blood deficiency with insomnia. Chicken warms the middle and tonifies Qi, suitable for postpartum, postsurgical, and chronic illness recovery.
Blood-Tonifying Foods

Angelica sinensis is the foremost Blood-tonifying herb. The Ben Cao Gang Mu describes it as "treating headaches and various abdominal pains, moistening the intestines, bones, and skin." Its unique property of both tonifying and activating Blood makes it distinctive among blood-tonifying foods. I often recommend that Blood-deficient patients stew 15 grams of Angelica with chicken or pork ribs weekly. Donkey-hide gelatin (Ejiao), made from donkey hide, has exceptionally prominent effects in tonifying Blood, nourishing Yin, moistening dryness, and stopping bleeding — it is the "trump card" herb for treating Blood deficiency patterns. However, its richness may impair digestive function, so those with weak Spleen and Stomach or poor digestion should not take it alone in large amounts — it should be combined with Qi-regulating and Spleen-strengthening herbs. Goji berries nourish the Liver and Kidney, benefit essence, and brighten the eyes — chewed or steeped as tea, they effectively tonify Blood and nourish the Liver, with 15 to 20 grams daily being optimal. Black sesame tonifies the Liver and Kidney and benefits essence and Blood — the Ben Cao Bei Yao records it as "tonifying the Liver and Kidney, moistening the five viscera, and replenishing marrow," suitable for long-term consumption. Pork liver tonifies the Liver and nourishes Blood, and spinach nourishes Blood and stops bleeding — cooking them together in soup provides excellent dietary therapy for iron-deficiency anemia.
6. Medicinal Food Recipes

Medicinal food represents the concentrated embodiment of the TCM principle of "applying medicine through diet," skillfully integrating therapeutic treatment with daily meals. The following three recipes are ones I frequently recommend to patients in clinical practice — they are easy to prepare at home, safe, and effective.

en.title: Angelica Astragalus Chicken Soup
en.instructions:
1. Cut chicken, blanch to remove blood
2. Rinse angelica and astragalus
3. Place all in clay pot, add water
4. Bring to boil, simmer 2 hours
5. Season with salt
6. Benefits: Tonifies Qi and Blood

en.text: This is the representative medicinal food for dual Qi-Blood tonification. Astragalus tonifies Qi, Angelica tonifies Blood, Red dates and Longan nourish Blood and calm the spirit, and the old hen warms the middle and tonifies Qi. In my clinical observation, patients with Qi-Blood deficiency who consume this soup once or twice weekly show marked improvement in complexion, energy levels, and physical strength after one month of consistent use.

en.title: Longan Red Date Porridge
en.instructions:
1. Soak rice 30 minutes
2. Wash longan and dates
3. Cook all together
4. Simmer 20 minutes
5. Add sugar
6. Benefits: Tonifies Heart-Spleen, calms spirit

en.title: Yam Goji Pork Rib Soup
en.instructions:
1. Blanch ribs
2. Peel and cut yam
3. Simmer ribs 1 hour
4. Add yam and goji, cook 20 more minutes
5. Season with salt
6. Benefits: Tonifies Qi-Yin, strengthens Spleen-Kidney

en.text: 7. Acupoint Massage for Qi-Blood

Acupoint massage is an indispensable aid for Qi-Blood tonification. Zusanli (ST36), located 3 cun below the knee on the lateral side of the leg, is the He-Sea point of the Stomach Meridian and one of the most important points for strengthening the body — as the saying goes, "massaging Zusanli regularly is better than eating old chicken." Pressing this point tonifies the middle Qi and strengthens the Spleen and Stomach. Qihai (CV6), located 1.5 cun below the navel on the midline of the abdomen, is where Yuan Qi converges — massaging with the palm in clockwise circles (36 rotations) powerfully tonifies Qi and consolidates the foundation. Xuehai (SP10), 2 cun above the medial border of the patella on the inner thigh, is a key point for regulating blood — pressing it tonifies and nourishes Blood while activating circulation and resolving stasis, particularly suitable for women with Blood deficiency and menstrual irregularities. Sanyinjiao (SP6), 3 cun above the medial malleolus on the medial leg, is the meeting point of the Liver, Spleen, and Kidney meridians — it is exceptionally effective for regulating and tonifying Qi and Blood and harmonizing the Liver and Kidney. Geshu (BL17), 1.5 cun lateral to the spinous process of the seventh thoracic vertebra, is the "Influential Point of Blood" among the Eight Influential Points, specializing in treating all blood-related conditions. Pressing each of these points for 1 to 2 minutes daily and maintaining consistent practice will significantly improve Qi and Blood circulation over time.
8. Lifestyle Recommendations

When it comes to regulating Qi and Blood, the importance of lifestyle rivals that of herbal medicine. The Su Wen established the general principle of health preservation: "regularity in diet and drink, constancy in daily routine, and avoidance of overexertion" — principles that remain the cornerstone of Qi-Blood regulation today. Regular sleep is the first essential — sleep before 11 PM and ensure 7 to 8 hours of high-quality sleep, as the night hours are the golden time for Qi and Blood repair and regeneration. Moderate exercise promotes the circulation of Qi and Blood, but those with Qi-Blood deficiency should avoid strenuous activities — gentle exercises such as walking, jogging, tai chi, and Ba Duan Jin are most suitable. Emotional balance cannot be overlooked — Liver Qi stagnation is a major trigger for Qi-Blood disharmony, and maintaining a cheerful disposition while avoiding excessive mental strain is a "free medicine." Meals should be regular and nutritionally balanced, with an emphasis on Qi-Blood tonifying foods. Balance work and rest to avoid overexertion. Moderate sun exposure aids vitamin D synthesis, benefiting calcium absorption and overall health.
9. Modern Research Support

The scientific basis of TCM Qi-Blood tonification is increasingly being revealed by modern research. Astragalus polysaccharides, the core active components of Astragalus, have been shown to enhance immune function and promote the proliferation and differentiation of hematopoietic stem cells, thereby improving anemic conditions. Ferulic acid in Angelica sinensis demonstrates clear antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and antiplatelet aggregation effects — findings that closely align with the traditional understanding of "Angelica tonifies and activates blood." Modern pharmacological studies of Donkey-hide gelatin (Ejiao) confirm that it promotes the generation of red blood cells and hemoglobin, increases serum iron levels, and has clear therapeutic effects on both iron-deficiency anemia and hemorrhage-induced anemia. Regarding acupoint massage, research indicates that stimulating points such as Zusanli can regulate the neuroendocrine system and improve both local and systemic microcirculation. These research findings provide modern scientific evidence for the TCM theory of Qi-Blood tonification and further confirm that TCM is a treasure trove worth deep exploration.

This content is for educational purposes only and should not replace professional medical diagnosis. Qi-Blood conditioning should be conducted under the guidance of a qualified TCM practitioner following proper pattern differentiation. Those with severe Qi-Blood deficiency should pursue medication-based treatment and not rely solely on dietary therapy and self-regulation.
